title: Creating Performance Metrics for Roles More About Quality
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership Field Note addresses how leaders can measure performance in roles where quality matters more than counting tasks. It argues that raw counts such as meetings run or projects closed reward the wrong behavior and fail to separate top performers from the rest. The proposed method starts with the people already operating at the highest standard and asks what they do differently to achieve high quality. The answers become observable dimensions of quality that can be calibrated by human judgment against real examples. Using a chief of staff as the worked example, the piece shows how each dimension turns into a trackable measure, such as how early issues surface or how often decisions stick. No single measure tells the whole story, but several observers applying the same anchored standards produce a reliable picture of excellence.
points: Counting tasks in quality-based roles can encourage shortcuts and rewards the wrong behavior, so activity counts are a poor proxy for excellence.
The route to a good metric begins with top performers: ask what they do differently, then define those dimensions more precisely.
Each dimension becomes a measure, for example the share of issues surfaced before they are urgent or the percentage of decisions that hold without being reopened.
Anchoring ratings in real examples from top performers turns subjective opinions into a shared standard that raters can calibrate against.
No single measure suffices, but several observers using the same anchored standards give leaders a defensible basis for rewarding the right people.
quotes: But some roles are more about quality than action. Others defy measurement because counting tasks can lead to shortcuts or lower quality.

The next step is to ask the question: “What are the top performers doing differently to achieve high quality?” The answer will guide leaders to the dimensions of quality that are worth defining more precisely so they can be calibrated by human judgment.
While counting meetings run or projects closed would be easy, it would reward the wrong behavior and fail to distinguish the top performers.
Anchored by examples from top performers, these judgments stop being opinions. They become a shared standard that tells everyone what excellence looks like.

No single measure tells the whole story, and each still relies on human judgment. But when several observers apply the same anchored standards and compare their ratings, a reliable picture of top performance emerges.
Roles built on quality will never yield simple metrics, but that does not leave leaders at the mercy of subjective opinions.
